# Course Description

The recent development of AI technologies has often been compared with the most profound technological revolutions in human civilization. There is no question that this technology has changed and will continue to change various aspects of our society in crucial ways. As social scientists, it is imperative for us to understand the most current state of this technology and situate its construction, development, and effects within the broader social context, leveraging the powerful social, political, and economic theories developed based on empirical and theoretical understanding of the historical incidents of social change. 

This minicourse focuses on the political economy of AI technologies, first by examining their effects on the labor market through the theoretical lens of technological change and automation in capitalistic societies. Then, we examine the infrastructure of the technologies: data, workers, capital, and resources, and the geopolitics that this technology is embedded in. Then, we spend a week that examines and discusses how to conceptualize and understand the impact of this technology on our daily life. In the end, we wrap up with a sociological examination of the AI tech elites and experts as a profession, and examine the development and collisions of their visions and ideologies of an "ideal world." 


# Learning Objectives

By the end of the minicourse, students are expected to: 

1. Understand the historical development and material foundation of the current AI technologies, including the basics of neural network vs. the expert system, the origin of the training data, the process of RLHF, data centers/hyperscalers, and the capital and energy resources involved in the scaling of the technology.
2. Develop understanding and hypotheses on the current wave of technological change by connecting it to theories of technological change, and be familiar with the cutting-edge methods and findings on AI's effects on the (domestic) labor market. 
3. Understand how AI is "sociological" through the reading of sociological analyses of the various aspects of the technology both before and after the rise of genAI, including (1) the politics of classification and knowledge production, (2) the various ways AI may alter social interactions and the cultural understanding of intelligence and of "machines," and (3) the rising power of the AI tech elites and the social and political implications of their values and visions of the technology. 
4. Evaluate how your existing research interest/research questions might be affected or should be adjusted given the development of AI technologies. Formulate new research questions related to AI.

## Discussion

This seminar is built on discussion, and therefore it is imperative for all students to participate actively in class discussion that critically engages with the course readings. **I expect students to come to class with questions and reflective thoughts**. Use the reading memo questions to guide yourself to prepare questions. Another great way to prepare questions/discussion points is to read other students' reading reflection memos before class and engage with them in class. 

## Memos

### Reading Reflection

From Week 2 to Week 7, pick two weeks and write reading memos based on that week's readings (**2-page max, single-spaced**). Submit the memo by **Tuesday 6 PM before the week's class to the shared [Google Folder](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Pyv6NlX1C5cp5bcocV_sV5wIap-EVvnm?usp=drive_link)**. For example, if you plan to write a memo for Week 3's class on Nov. 4th, you should submit your memo by 6 PM, Tuesday Nov. 3rd. The memos should address the following questions:

1. What is the central theme, question, or debate of this week's reading?
2. How do the readings approach the question differently and how do their findings/arguments connect (or not)? Feel free to draw connections to earlier weeks' readings if relevant. 
3. What is your critical evaluation of the readings? What gaps or questions do you think are promising and important to pursue but are left out?

You are encouraged to read each other's memos before class and engage with the ideas proposed in these memos for class discussions. 

### Course Reflection

At the end of the class, every student should submit a course reflection memo (**3-page max, single-spaced**). This is due by **Monday, Dec. 14th at 11:59 PM via Canvas Assignment**. It should address the following questions: 

1. What have you learned about AI technology from this minicourse? Which one(s) are most important to you and why? 
2. What aspect of AI is sociological? In your view, what are the central questions and research agenda that a "sociology of AI" should pursue? 
3. Evaluate whether your existing research interest and research questions are affected by what you have learned in this minicourse. In addition, what new questions do you think are worth pursuing? 

---

- Follow the **AI Usage Policy** below for your memo writing. 
- Late submission will be given a 10% penalty per hour unless otherwise noted. 


# AI Usage Policy

**AI writing is strictly prohibited in this class. You are not allowed to use AI for writing memos for this course.** Writing and thinking are intrinsically linked, and the process of finding the language to express your ideas (even if it is summarizing others' arguments) is essential for producing original and creative research.

I understand that if English is your second language (which is the case for me), you might lack confidence in the quality of your writing. You can use AI tools (or Grammarly) to correct the following grammar mistakes: subject–verb agreement, verb tense consistency within a clause, pronoun–antecedent agreement, article errors, and spelling errors. However, **you cannot use AI to polish or rewrite any part of your writing assignments.** It is okay if your sentences are rough. I'd rather you write them down than delegate writing tasks to AI.

A particular challenge in responsible AI use in higher education is *enforcement*. While there are plenty of AI detection tools, there is no guarantee that they will not make mistakes, and any false positives will likely result in unfair accusation. As the course instructor, **I acknowledge the limitations of these AI detection technologies, but reserve the right to check your writing using such tools when in doubt.** I also reserve the right to request additional oral exams if I suspect the use of AI in your writing assignments. If you feel uncomfortable about the possibility that your writing might be uploaded to AI detection tools, please come talk to me and we can find a different arrangement. 

The general rule of thumb is **not to automate the process of learning, thinking, and writing to AI,** which means you should always read and puzzle with the literature yourself, rather than let an LLM summarize it for you without reading it directly.

# Additional Resources

I recommend the following books — most of them are already in our required readings, but we only read part of them, and I recommend reading them in full if the topic is of interest to you. In addition, there are three special issues on the sociology of AI that curate some cutting-edge research that sociologists are pursuing. I recommend checking them out, too. 

## Books

- Bostrom, Nick. 2016. *Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies*. Oxford University Press.
- Crawford, Kate. 2021. *Atlas of AI: Power, Politics, and the Planetary Costs of Artificial Intelligence*. Yale University Press.
- Hao, Karen. 2025. *Empire of AI: Dreams and Nightmares in Sam Altman’s OpenAI*. Penguin Press.
- Kasy, Maximilian. 2025. *The Means of Prediction: How AI Really Works (and Who Benefits)*. University of Chicago Press.
- Mitchell, Melanie. (2019) 2025. *Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans*. Picador.
- Srnicek, Nick. 2026. *Silicon Empires: The Fight for the Future of AI*. Polity.

# Course Expectations and Policies

## Mutual Respect and Privacy

In this course, we will encounter a variety of important debates pertaining to the use and impacts of new technologies. Some may touch on contentious subjects and/or spotlight harms that may be especially concentrated within certain communities. I expect students to engage with each other's perspectives respectfully and constructively. I hope that discussions will be rigorous, but also ask that we work together to build an inclusive classroom environment.

In the interest of creating a comfortable environment for sharing questions, ideas, and experiences in class discussions, I ask that you not make any digital recordings (audio, photographic, or video) of others without their consent during class time, unless that is part of your academic accommodations. Also, check in with me before sharing any course materials with others outside of this class.

## Academic Integrity

Academic integrity means that the work you submit is original. See Rutgers University–New Brunswick's [Academic Integrity Policy](https://nbacademicintegrity.rutgers.edu). You should also follow this course's AI Usage Policy.

## Office Hours and Email Availability

I will hold office hours at the times listed at the top of this syllabus. If these times don't work for you, please email me to arrange an alternate time. As a general practice, I will respond to emails within 24 hours during the week. If I do not respond within two business days, please send me an email as a reminder.

## Accommodations

Students who require accommodation to level the playing field can contact the [Rutgers Office of Disability Services (ODS)](https://ods.rutgers.edu). However, I also recognize that not all forms of challenges may receive official accommodations and navigating university bureaucracy can be difficult. Please reach out to me at any time and let me know how I can support you to make course requirements and challenges manageable.

## Wellness Statement

In a large, complex community like Rutgers University, it is vital to reach out to others, particularly those who are isolated or engaged in self-destructive activities. Student wellness is the responsibility of us all. [Rutgers Counseling, ADAP & Psychiatric Services (CAPS)](https://health.rutgers.edu/counseling-services) (848-932-7402) is the office responsible for the overall health and mental health needs of Rutgers–New Brunswick students. For 24/7 crisis support and additional resources, see [go.rutgers.edu/mentalhealthresources](http://go.rutgers.edu/mentalhealthresources).
